KEYWORDS
GPGPU, Nvidia, Intel ARC, OpenCL, Automatic-Tuning.
ABSTRACT
This article analyses the usability of Intel ARC 770 based
on Intel Xe Architecture for scientific computational tasks
based on the Numerical Integration in Finite Element
Method (FEM). To achieve a thorough comparison, we
employed our proprietary auto-tuning algorithm, allowing
us to assess architectural differences between Intel’s so-
lution and the widely adopted Nvidia architecture. As a
reference point, we selected the GeForce RTX 3060 Lap-
top due to its comparable performance and similar price
at the time of release. Intel’s latest GPU architecture rep-
resents a significant step in the company’s ongoing efforts
to establish a foothold in the GPGPU market, challenging
Nvidia’s longstanding dominance. While our benchmark-
ing results indicate that the ARC 770 delivers performance
on par with reference Nvidia architecture, we identified
distinctive behavioural characteristics that set it apart from
previously analyzed architectures. These unique attributes
could affect computational efficiency and workload distri-
bution, making Intel’s approach an intriguing alternative
for scientific computing. Through a series of experiments
and simulations, we aim to provide deeper insight into
how architectural variations influence the efficiency of
FEM numerical integration. Given that the tested Intel
GPU shares similarities with the professional Xe-HPC
lineup, our research also explores its potential applicabil-
ity beyond consumer-grade hardware, positioning it as a
viable option for high-performance computing tasks.
INTRODUCTION
We can observe several hardware and software design
strategies in modern scientific computing. The first lies
in the increasing number of computing cores, while the
second focuses on providing specialized units called ac-
celerators, usually based on GPU architecture. Using
accelerators for scientific computation is a necessity in
modern times because fast and accurate results can be ob-
tained only by using such hardware. Fortunately, in most
cases, for simulation and testing purposes, one can use the
cheapest versions of the professional accelerators by using
the gaming graphics cards because most of the hardware
vendors provide both - the less expensive GPUs for the
general public use, as well as the professional expensive
accelerator cards, based on the similar structure and the
same architecture, extended for the more demanding tasks.
The graphics card market has long been dominated by
two major players, Nvidia and AMD, whose GPU-based
accelerators share a similar architecture centred around
arrays of stream processors organized into multiprocessor
units. In response to the expanding demand for external
accelerators, Intel, a leader in general-purpose processor
manufacturing, ventured into this domain by developing
the Intel Many Integrated Core (MIC) architecture. This
architecture was implemented in the Intel Xeon Phi co-
processors, codenamed Knights Corner (KNC), aiming
to merge CPUs’ programming ease with GPUs’ compu-
tational prowess. The Intel Xeon Phi became integral to
numerous high-performance computing systems. By June
2015, approximately 34% of the world’s top 500 super-
computers incorporated this type of accelerator. How-
ever, literature frequently cited a significant drawback: the
performance gains did not always justify the extensive
code optimization required for these accelerators (Rosales,
2013). Consequently, Intel officially discontinued the
Xeon Phi line (Intel Corporation, July 23, 2018). Building
upon the lessons from Xeon Phi, Intel introduced the Xe
graphics architecture in November 2019. This new archi-
tecture sought to rectify previous shortcomings by offering
a unified programming model through the Intel oneAPI
programming framework and delivering enhanced perfor-
mance (Intel Corporation, 2019). The Intel Xe family
encompasses various microarchitectures tailored to dis-
tinct applications: Xe-LP (Low Power) for integrated and
energy-efficient solutions, Xe-HPG (High-Performance
Gaming) for gaming, Xe-HP (High Performance) for data
centres and artificial intelligence workloads and Xe-HPC
(High-Performance Computing) for supercomputing appli-
cations (Smith, 2020). Intel claims that its Xe architecture
represents a significant evolution from the Xeon Phi era,
and it can be a significant player in the all-wide GPU mar-
ket, which we try to check by testing the widely-common
scientific numerical integration algorithm with the use of

this architecture (Cutress, 2019). In this context, as of
November 2024, the Aurora supercomputer built by Intel
is ranked 3rd in the world. The system is based on the HPE
Cray EX architecture with Intel Xeon CPU Max Series
processors and Intel Data Centre GPU Max Series accel-
erators (Strohmaier et al., 2020). The test results from
the Aurora supercomputer confirm that the Intel Xe-HPC
architecture is competitive with other solutions available
in the HPC market. Aurora’s achievement of exascale
performance and its position at the top of the TOP500
list testify to Intel’s ability to deliver high-performance
computing solutions (Chustecki, 2024). Intel Data Center
GPU Max Series is engineered for data centres and HPC
environments, but it is based on almost the same architec-
ture as Intel ARC A770. That is why Intel ARC770 can
be treated as an accessible entry point for developers and
researchers to familiarize themselves with Intel’s GPU
architecture. By experimenting with the A770, users can
gain insights into the Xe architecture’s capabilities, facil-
itating a smoother transition to deploying workloads on
Data Center GPU Max Series accelerators when scaling
up is required. The Arc A770 offers a consumer-friendly
platform that mirrors the architectural principles of Intel’s
professional accelerators. It provides a practical pathway
for those aiming to scale their applications to enterprise-
level deployments. The main difference between today’s
GPU-based accelerators lies in the multi-level memory
handling. While the main problem of the external comput-
ing units is the interface bottleneck between the external
accelerator’s memory and the host system’s RAM, the
different architectures have different ways of using the
multi-level memory hierarchy within the card itself. De-
pending on the architecture and the software, this can lead
to different performance characteristics. The main aim
of our studies is to research the best potential use of the
memory hierarchy for different architectures. For this pur-
pose, we have developed the auto-tuning mechanism for
the FEM numerical integration algorithm. This allows us
to test different data usage strategies on many different
architectures. Our previous studies include modern graph-
ics processors (Bana´s et al., 2020), CPUs (Kru˙zel, 2019),
hybrid systems (Kru˙zel and Bana´s, 2015), as well as Intel
Xeon Phi (Bana´s and Kru˙zel, 2014; Kru˙zel et al., 2023).
This article is a direct successor to our previous studies
on the Intel Xe architecture based on Xe-LP used in the
integrated chips in modern Intel CPUs (Kru˙zel and Nytko,
2024).
NUMERICAL INTEGRATION ALGORITHM

computations remains one of the most demanding chal-
lenges in computational engineering. One of the key as-
pects of FEM, numerical integration, plays a crucial role
in constructing elementary stiffness matrices, which are
essential for the final solver. A detailed discussion of
numerical integration principles can be found in our previ-
ous studies (Bana´s et al., 2020; Kru˙zel and Nytko, 2022;
Kru˙zel, 2019).

We refined the conventional integration formula to stan-
dardise and enhance mathematical computations, formu-
lating a generalised numerical integration algorithm for
finite elements of the same type and approximation degree
(Alg. 1). The algorithm’s design ensures adaptability by
allowing loop structure modifications and memory usage
flexibility for storing computational arrays. These features
enabled us to develop an automated system for algorithm
optimisation tailored to various hardware accelerators,
such as GPUs, APUs or FPGAs. In our simulations, we
employed two commonly used physical problems to test
different hardware’s memory and computational capabili-
ties comprehensively. The first one is based on the stan-
dard Poisson equation, which can be used, for example, to
simulate stationary temperature distribution. The second is
the artificial convection-diffusion-reaction problem, incor-
porating a nonzero problem coefficient matrix C to intro-
duce additional computational complexity. We used pris-


matic elements to challenge the numerical performance,
offering superior geometric fidelity for complex computa-
tional domains Ω(Kallinderis, 1995). Compared to linear
tetrahedral elements, prismatic elements are computation-
ally more expensive, making them a suitable benchmark
for the performance evaluation of different hardware.
HARDWARE
In our previous research, we focused on Intel’s new line
of Intel Iris GPUs. Initially, we used the Iris Xe-LP based
on the Tiger Lake architecture integrated with the Intel i7
11370H processor, comparing it to the Nvidia GeForce
3060 Laptop graphics system, which allowed us to exam-
ine the impact of SVM on the calculation process. Con-
tinuing our research, we compared two consecutive Intel
graphics architectures - Tiger Lake and Alder Lake. As a
result of the tests, we observed that despite the increase in
computing power in the newer unit, the simultaneous re-
duction in memory bandwidth has a significant impact on
the performance of calculations that are strongly related
to memory access. In this article, we use a dedicated Intel
ARC 770 card - a unit based on the Alchemist architec-
ture, the aim of which is to directly compete with graphics
cards from manufacturers such as Nvidia and AMD in the
mid and mid-high segment.
Intel ARC 770
The Arc A770 graphics card used in our research is the
most efficient unit on Intel’s offer. The Alchemist architec-
ture significantly differs from the Intel Xe-LP family inte-
grated graphics architectures used in our previous research.
The most significant difference between an integrated and
a dedicated graphics system is the change in the grouping
structure of computing units. In Intel Xe-LP, 16 execution
units (EU) are grouped into subslices, the total number
of which is 6, which gives 96 EUs on the whole chip.
In Xe-HPG 16, Vector Engines (previously EU) creates
Xe-Core (previously subslice). Four Xe-Cores make up
Render Slice, of which there are 8 in Arc A770, ultimately
giving 512 Vector Engines (Fig. 1). The full specifications

METHODOLOGY
ModFEM
In our experiments, we used ModFEM, a modular soft-
ware platform based on the finite element method for en-
gineering computations (Michalik et al., 2013). Thanks to
its modular design, the platform enables the customisation
of various aspects of finite element analysis, including
approximation, mesh management, and solving the final
system of equations. The software consists of multiple
hierarchical levels, each incorporating distinct modules.
Among them, the problems module serves as the primary
user-managed component, allowing for the definition of
FEM weak formulations and the integration of other es-
sential modules. As part of our research, we have used our
previously developed extension to the approximation mod-
ule, which supports hardware acceleration. This extension
provides support for various frameworks like CUDA and
OpenCL. Additionally, adjustments were made to the prob-
lem modules relevant to the investigated tasks to facilitate
the proper data structuring and comparative testing of the
numerical integration algorithm for using the automatic
parameter tuning mechanism implemented over all mod-
ules of the ModFEM.
OpenCL
OpenCL was used as the main programming framework
for the auto-tuning mechanism. OpenCL is a flexible and
widely used approach among various accelerator program-
ming methods. It supports numerous modern architec-
tures, including GPUs and coprocessors such as Xeon Phi
or even the specialised cores in the heterogeneous CPUs.
The OpenCL memory model categorises multiple memory
regions that programmers can utilise. Its design reflects
the physical structure of typical GPU memory, as OpenCL
was developed initially for GPU programming. Due to its
portability, each memory object can be mapped differently
based on the available hardware resources. Variables de-
clared within a kernel reside in private memory and are
stored in scalar or vector registers, while other memory
types are designated using specific qualifiers. OpenCL de-
fines three key memory types: global, constant, and shared
(local). Traditionally, OpenCL computations required
transferring necessary data from the host to the device
memory. This process involved preparing memory buffers
on the host and employing various hardware or system-
level solutions to move data to the accelerator. Shared
Virtual Memory (SVM) in OpenCL 2.0 addressed these
challenges by improving the OpenCL memory model. In
our previous research, we have examined the usability
of OpenCL SVM in both integrated and discrete GPUs
(Kru˙zel and Nytko, 2023, 2024). While SVM covers the
problem of transferring the data from the host to GPU
memory and back, multi-level memory hierarchies still
rely on the GPUs’ internal structure. The way of handling
this memory differentiates hardware vendors, which is
why the same code does not provide performance porting
when running on different hardware. Because of that, we
have developed our automatic parameter-tuning mecha-
nism for the ModFEM framework. It provides the best
performance of our numerical integration-based bench-
mark on each tested architecture. Additionally, it gives
detailed remarks about what parameters play a crucial role
in achieving the best performance on specific hardware.


In this study, we tested the Intel ARC770 GPU and com-
pared its behaviour with the more widely popular Nvidia
solution, such as the Geforce RTX 3060M GPU. Both
cards have similar specifications and achieve similar per-
formance in the commonly available benchmark, which
makes them the perfect material for detailed study with
our code.
Auto-Tuning
Our automatic parameter tuning is based on various param-
eters crucial in managing the data stored on the accelerator.
The first parameter is WORKGROUP SIZE, which is re-
lated to the minimum number of threads possible to launch
on the accelerator. In our case, a standard value of 64 is
recommended for most GPU-based accelerators. The fol-
lowing two adjustable parameters determine the method
for reading from and writing to the accelerator’s memory.
Given the physical architecture of such devices and the
organization of threads into groups, memory access pat-
terns can significantly influence algorithm performance.
In the most popular Nvidia and AMD architectures, for
achieving optimal efficiency, memory access should be
structured to align with thread grouping, ensuring that
read and write operations occur continuously (coalesced)
and allowing entire data vectors to be processed at once.
During our experiments, we will check if these parameters
are also important in the case of Intels’ architecture. The
following parameter determines if the values of all shape
functions and their derivatives should be computed before
entering the double loop after the shape functions (line 9
of algorithm 1. The following four parameters are steering
the location of each possible array from the algorithm -
respectively, problem coefficients (line 4 of the algorithm
1), geometric data(line 5 of algorithm 1), data of shape
functions and their derivatives (lines 2 and 9 of algorithm
1) and local stiffness matrices and right-hand-side vec-
tors (line 6 of algorithm 1). This set of parameters in the
auto-tuning system primarily focuses on memory man-
agement within the OpenCL model, which is designed
around GPU architecture. Arrays passed as arguments to
the numerical integration procedure, such as geometric
data and problem coefficients, can be accessed directly
during computations or preloaded into local arrays stored
in registers or shared memory. Utilizing shared memory
as a temporary data buffer allows for continuous data read-
ing, where each thread sequentially retrieves a memory
cell and stores it in the shared buffer. The retrieved data
can then be retained in the buffer for later computations
or transferred to registers, freeing up the buffer for subse-
quent use. Since some of the parameters cannot be used
simultaneously, the total number of combinations for any
architecture is 40. Additionally, we can modify the al-
gorithm structure by changing the order of the leading
three loops - one over Gauss points and two over shape
functions - we call these versions QSS, SQS, and SSQ.
This kind of optimization is called loop interchange and is
very hard to use by automatic compiler optimizations, and
can significantly improve performance (Johnny’s Software
Lab, 2024). Considering this, there are three algorithm
variants (QSS, SQS, and SSQ) for each architecture and
two tasks to process, so the total number of combinations
per architecture reaches 240. The developed system com-
prises a collection of scripts and code segments that are
responsible for compiling the kernel with the appropriate
configuration settings. Given the variability in compilation
options provided by different software vendors, it was nec-
essary to adapt the implementation based on the installed
accelerator and the specific version of the OpenCL frame-
work. The more detailed information on the auto-tuning
mechanism can be found in (Bana´s et al., 2020). The auto-
mated tuning system provides an in-depth evaluation of the
Intel ARC770, assessing its suitability for scientific com-
putations, particularly in applications such as numerical
integration and the finite element method. This approach
enables a comprehensive analysis of performance charac-
teristics, ensuring optimal parameter selection for efficient
execution of computational tasks.
RESULTS
Poisson problem
In our first simulation, we run our auto-tuning mechanism
for the computational-easy Poisson problem. The results
of these tests can be seen in figure 3.
Figure 3: Auto-tuning of the Poisson problem on Intel
ARC770
We observe high peaks for the SSQ version of the al-
gorithm, which is expected because of the high memory
demand in this loop type. As observed, QSS and SQS
present similar times, but both SQS and SSQ seem more
stable. The main peaks in the inverted loop versions are
connected with the third auto-tuning option, which is the
precomputation of all the values of all shape functions
and their derivatives. The rest of the parameters do not
play a unique role in the SSQ and SQS versions. This
stable characteristic is a characteristic feature of most of
the GPUs we have tested, which means that in opposite
to the integrated Intel Xe-LP solution, ARC770 behaves
more like the Nvidia and AMD GPUs and not like CPU
or Intel Xeon Phi (Kru˙zel and Nytko, 2022). Although the
results were more chaotic, the QSS version obtained the
best times for most auto-tuning scenarios. That is why we


have used this version for comparison with the best QSS
version run on the reference RTX 3060 card (Fig 4).
Figure 4: Comparison of the auto-tuning of the ARC770
and RTX 3060 Laptop in Poisson problem
As we can see from the graph, the results of the auto-
tuning for Intel’s hardware seem more chaotic, while the
Nvidia one is strictly related to the coalesced writing of
the data to the memory. In Intel’s case, we can observe
the problems in data storage in shared memory, which
is quite surprising because ARC770 allocates a higher
amount of shared memory than Nvidia (64KB vs 48KB).

As observed in the best configuration results, coalesced
writing plays a significant role in optimizing performance
on Intel’s architecture, further reinforcing the idea that this
GPU follows a more conventional GPU memory model
compared to its predecessor, Intel Xeon Phi, which had a
more CPU-like architecture (Kru˙zel et al., 2023). Addi-
tionally, precomputing all shape functions and their deriva-
tives before entering the main loops does not appear to
be a crucial factor for Intel’s architecture, in contrast to
Nvidia’s GPUs, where this approach significantly impacts
performance. One particularly interesting finding is that
Intel Xe architecture does not rely on shared memory to
achieve peak performance. Instead, the larger available L1
cache (192KB total, with 64KB reserved for shared mem-
ory) and the substantial L2 cache (16MB) seems to enable
the buffering of all necessary computational data, reducing
memory access latency and ultimately improving compu-
tational efficiency. However, the validity of these conclu-
sions requires further verification on a more memory- and
computation-intensive problem, such as the convection-
diffusion-reaction equation, which presents greater chal-
lenges for both numerical integration and cache utilization.
Convection-diffusion problem
The results of the auto-tuning process for the convection-
diffusion problem are presented in figure 5. The SQS and
SSQ algorithms exhibit characteristics that are almost iden-
tical to those observed in the previous case. However, the
most notable observation concerns the QSS algorithm—in
this more demanding scenario, its performance appears
more stable and predictable, suggesting improved consis-
tency under increased computational load. As observed
Figure 5: Auto-tuning of the convection-diffusion
problem on Intel ARC770
in the comparison graph (Fig. 6), there are only three
distinct peaks, all of which are associated with two key
factors: the absence of coalesced memory access (both
reading and writing) and the additional computational
cost of generating shape functions and their derivatives,
which requires extra memory space for storing geometric
data or stiffness matrices. This pattern suggests that, in
this case, the time spent on additional computations can
significantly impact overall numerical integration perfor-
mance, introducing delays. More importantly, it indicates
that in Intel’s architecture, memory handling appears to
be more efficient than raw computational performance.
This insight raises an intriguing possibility—Intel’s solu-
tion could be particularly well-suited for memory-bound
scientific computations, where efficient data access and
buffering play a more critical role than sheer processing
power.


Figure 6: Comparison of the auto-tuning of the ARC770
and RTX 3060 Laptop in convection-diffusion problem
Based on the results presented in table 6, the Intel GPU
consistently outperforms the Nvidia GPU across all three
tested algorithms, achieving significantly lower execution
times and demonstrating greater efficiency in these nu-
merical computations. The largest performance gap is
observed in the SSQ algorithm, where the Intel GPU exe-
cutes it 2.55 times faster than the Nvidia counterpart. This
suggests that SSQ is highly memory-sensitive, and Intel’s
superior memory management or cache hierarchy may pro-
vide a significant advantage in this case. In contrast, the
QSS algorithm, which is less reliant on memory and more
dependent on raw computational power, shows a smaller
performance difference between the two GPUs. This con-
firms our previous observations that Nvidia’s architecture
is more competitive in compute-intensive scenarios, where
memory bandwidth plays a lesser role.

Nvidia’s compute-focused architecture still remains com-
petitive in purely computational workloads. This suggests
that the optimal choice of hardware strongly depends on
the specific characteristics of the numerical problem being
solved.
CONCLUSIONS
Our study demonstrates that the Intel ARC 770 excels
in memory-intensive workloads, outperforming Nvidia’s
GPU, particularly in algorithms where efficient memory
access is crucial. The larger L1 cache (128KB available)
and L2 cache (16MB) in Intel’s architecture enable bet-
ter data buffering, reducing reliance on shared memory
and minimising latency. Notably, in the SSQ algorithm,
where memory access patterns play a significant role, the
Intel ARC 770 achieved speeds up to 2.55 times faster
than the Nvidia RTX 3060 Laptop. However, in compute-
heavy workloads, such as the QSS algorithm, Nvidia re-
mained competitive, suggesting that Intel’s strength lies
in memory-bound rather than pure computation-bound
tasks. These findings indicate that Intel’s GPU architec-
ture could be a viable alternative for scientific applications,
particularly in workloads prioritising efficient data han-
dling over raw computational power. While these results
are promising, further research is needed to validate the
Intel ARC 770’s scalability in more complex scientific
problems, such as the discontinuous Galerkin approxima-
tion of higher-order elements. Additionally, comparisons
with higher-end Nvidia GPUs would provide a more com-
prehensive performance assessment. Intel’s latest GPU
architecture demonstrates strong potential in scientific
computing, particularly for memory-bound tasks. While
Nvidia retains an edge in raw computational performance,
the Intel ARC 770’s superior memory handling presents
a compelling alternative for applications requiring effi-
cient data movement. Future research will refine these
conclusions and explore the full potential of Intel’s Xe
architecture in high-performance computing.

Abstract: This article analyses the usability of Intel ARC 770 based on Intel Xe Architecture for scientific computational tasks based on the Numerical Integration in Finite Element Method (FEM). To achieve a thorough comparison, we employed our proprietary auto-tuning algorithm, allowing us to assess architectural differences between Intel’s so- lution and the widely adopted Nvidia architecture. As a reference point, we selected the GeForce RTX 3060 Lap- top due to its comparable performance and similar price at the time of release. Intel’s latest GPU architecture rep- resents a significant step in the company’s ongoing efforts to establish a foothold in the GPGPU market, challenging Nvidia’s longstanding dominance. While our benchmark- ing results indicate that the ARC 770 delivers performance on par with reference Nvidia architecture, we identified distinctive behavioural characteristics that set it apart from previously analyzed architectures. These unique attributes could affect computational efficiency and workload distri- bution, making Intel’s approach an intriguing alternative for scientific computing. Through a series of experiments and simulations, we aim to provide deeper insight into how architectural variations influence the efficiency of FEM numerical integration. Given that the tested Intel GPU shares similarities with the professional Xe-HPC lineup, our research also explores its potential applicabil- ity beyond consumer-grade hardware, positioning it as a viable option for high-performance computing tasks.
